newsitem.title: UK: IEA regrets German oil sale, sees disturbing trend.
newsitem.headline: IEA regrets German oil sale, sees disturbing trend.

text.p: The International Energy Agency (IEA) said it deeply regretted reports from Bonn on Thursday that the German government had decided to sell 400 million marks worth of oil from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve.

Robert Priddle, executive director of the Paris-based IEA, said in a statement that Germany's decision did not jeopardise the IEA's energy security programme because other oil stocks in the country would provide more than 90 days for net imports - the minimum quantity that all IEA member states are committed to maintain.
But he said in the statement that the decision continued a disturbing trend of lower oil stocks.
"The IEA deeply regrets reports from Bonn today that the German government has decided to sell...oil from its Strategic Petroleum Reserves (SPRs)," Priddle said.
"The reported decision by Bonn -- coupled with the series of recent and forthcoming American sales -- sets a regrettable example to other IEA members."
The U.S. government has drawn down its strategic stocks three times in the last 18 months and legislation now before the U.S. congress would authorise a further sale of $209 million worth of oil.

Following that stock reduction in the United States the IEA calculates that the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve will stand below 70 days of net imports. Several other IEA members have allowed stocks to dip slightly below the 90-day level.

If member countries were to continue selling off strategic oil reserves in order to minimise their budget deficits they would eventually undermine the highly successful energy security programme initiated by the IEA after the first "oil shock" in 1974, the statement said.
This programme has kept member countries prepared to counter emergencies in the oil market for 23 years.
It fully proved its value during the Gulf War in 1991. At that time IEA members drew on reserve stocks and placed them on the market.
Germany participated in the successful action of 1991. Germany is the IEA's third largest importer and the third largest holder of energy stocks - 10 percent of the total.
The reported decision by Bonn -- coupled with the series of recent and forthcoming U.S. -- sets a regrettable example to other IEA members, the statement added.
It also sends confusing signals to those non-member countries which are considering active co-operation with the IEA to enhance global energy security.

Priddle said in the statement he was confident that Germany and other member states would recognise the importance of retaining and reinforcing a security programme that has worked extremely well over almost a quarter of a century.

He said ministers meeting in Paris two months ago formally reiterated that "energy security remains the most important criterion guiding IEA activities" while stressing the need to maintain and improve the level of emergency stocks.
With a certain prescience the ministers also warned that there was "no room for complacency" on oil security issues. Priddle said he urged them and their governments to heed that sound advice.
